A reproducible technical note

Filters: from pen and paper to 3D

One idea — predict, then correct with data — from a scalar you can work out by hand to the Kalman, extended, unscented and particle filters, and three real 3D problems: radar tracking, GNSS positioning, and data assimilation.
Dr. Dipak Munshi  ·  Advanced Research Fellow, Imperial College London  ·  part of the ML & Stat Notes series  ·  every figure generated by the code described here
Bayesian filteringKalman EKF / UKFparticle filter radar trackingGNSS / PNT data assimilation

Abstract

A filter keeps a running best estimate of something that is changing, using a stream of noisy measurements. The whole subject is one recursion repeated forever: predict where the state goes next (and let the uncertainty grow), then update that guess with the latest measurement (and let the uncertainty shrink). This note builds the idea from the ground up. We start with a single number you can filter with a pencil, write down every step of the Kalman filter and watch its gain and variance settle; move to the matrix form and track a moving object in 2D from position alone; then meet the three ways of coping when the world is nonlinear or non-Gaussian — the extended (EKF), unscented (UKF) and particle filters — each the same recursion with one honest approximation. The payoff is three genuine 3D problems solved with worked code: radar tracking of a target from range/azimuth/elevation, GNSS positioning of a receiver from satellite pseudoranges, and data assimilation of a chaotic 3D system with the ensemble Kalman filter — the same machinery that keeps weather models on track. Small 1D and 2D examples make every idea concrete; the recurring lesson is that a filter is only as honest as its noise models, and knowing which filter to reach for is mostly knowing which approximation your problem can afford.

Here is a problem you solve without thinking. You are watching something move — a plane on a radar screen, your position on a map, the temperature of a room — and every reading is a little wrong. You do not believe each reading on its own, and you do not ignore them either; you blend what you expected to see with what you actually measured, and you trust the blend more than either part. That blend, made precise, is a filter. This note is about how to do it properly: from a scalar worked by hand up to three-dimensional tracking, navigation and forecasting, with the code that produced every figure.

1The idea: predict, then correct

Every filter in this note is the same two-step loop. Learn it once.

We assume a state — the thing we want to know (a position, a velocity, a temperature) — that evolves in time, and measurements that depend on it but are corrupted by noise. The classic linear-Gaussian model is

The state-space model

is the dynamics (how the state moves on its own), is the measurement map (how the state shows up in the sensor), is the process noise (how much the state can surprise us) and is the measurement noise (how much the sensor lies). Everything we know about is carried as a Gaussian: a mean and a covariance .

Why a physicist should care

This is Bayes' rule run in real time. The predict step is the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation (push a density through the dynamics); the update step is Bayes' theorem (multiply prior by likelihood). A filter is just the posterior maintained recursively, so you never have to store or reprocess the whole history. That recursion is what makes real-time estimation possible at all — on a radar, in a phone, inside a weather model.

2The 1D Kalman filter, by hand

One number, two equations per step. You can do this with a pencil.

Take the simplest case: the state is a single number that drifts slowly (a random walk, ), and we measure it directly with noise (). Then and the covariances are scalars and . The recursion collapses to four lines:

The scalar Kalman filter

Predict:  ,    (mean unchanged, variance grows).
Update:  ,   ,   .

The gain is the whole story. It is a number between 0 and 1 that says how much to trust the new measurement. If the sensor is perfect () then and we jump straight to the measurement. If the sensor is useless () then and we keep our prediction. In between, is exactly the fraction .

Let us actually turn the handle. With process noise and measurement noise , starting from and , the first update step reads: predict gives ; the gain is ; a measurement moves the estimate to ; and the variance drops to . Two steps later — the filter already trusts its own prediction more than any single noisy reading, because it has accumulated information. Left to run, and settle to constants (, ): a steady state where each new measurement buys the same small amount of certainty.

In code (the whole filter is the loop)

Q, R = 0.01, 0.25            # process- and measurement-noise variances
xh, P = z[0], R              # initialise from the first measurement
for k in range(1, N):
    # --- predict ---
    xp = xh                  # random walk: mean unchanged
    Pp = P + Q               # variance grows by Q
    # --- update ---
    K  = Pp / (Pp + R)       # Kalman gain: 0 = ignore data, 1 = believe it
    xh = xp + K * (z[k] - xp)
    P  = (1 - K) * Pp

That is the entire Kalman filter in one dimension. Everything else in this note is this loop with as matrices, or with a trick for handling nonlinearity.

3Many dimensions: tracking in 2D

The same four lines, now with vectors and matrices — and the magic of inferring what you never measured.

Real states have several components. To track a moving object we keep position and velocity, , even though a position sensor only measures the first two. The dynamics say “new position = old position + velocity”, and the measurement picks off position:

Constant-velocity model

The general recursion is the matrix version of the scalar one:

Predict:  ,   .
Update:  (the innovation),   ,   ,   ,   .

The beautiful part is in the cross-terms of . Because position and velocity become correlated through the dynamics, a measurement of position also corrects the velocity estimate. The filter infers a quantity it never directly observes — it reads velocity out of the pattern of position measurements, exactly as your eye does when it sees where a thrown ball is going.

4When the world is nonlinear: the EKF

Most real sensors are nonlinear. The oldest fix: linearize.

The Kalman filter is exact only when and are linear. But a radar does not measure Cartesian position — it measures range , azimuth and elevation, all nonlinear functions of the state. A GNSS receiver measures distances to satellites, also nonlinear. The Extended Kalman Filter handles this the way calculus handles any curve: replace it, locally, by its tangent.

The EKF idea

Keep nonlinear functions and for the actual predict and innovation, but use their Jacobians (matrices of partial derivatives) wherever the Kalman equations need or : Then run the ordinary Kalman update with these local linearizations. The predicted measurement is , the innovation is , and as before.

What does linearizing cost? A straight line cannot capture a curve's bend, so pushing a Gaussian through the tangent gives the wrong spread — and a biased mean. The picture below makes this exact for : the tangent at the mean has slope , so the EKF reports , but the true pushed mean is — a bias of exactly that the EKF simply does not see. With the EKF puts the mean at while the truth sits at . When the curve is nearly straight over this is harmless; when it bends sharply, the EKF grows overconfident.

5A smarter nonlinear filter: the UKF

Don't linearize the function — sample it at a few clever points.

The Unscented Kalman Filter rests on a simple observation: it is easier to approximate a probability distribution than an arbitrary nonlinear function. Instead of differentiating , it picks a small set of deterministic sigma points that exactly carry the current mean and covariance, pushes each one through the true nonlinear map, and reads the output mean and covariance back off the transformed points. No Jacobians, no derivatives — just a handful of function evaluations.

The unscented transform

For an -dimensional Gaussian , form sigma points using a matrix square root of (via Cholesky): push them through the map, , and recombine with weights : The weights are chosen so that for a linear this reproduces the exact Kalman answer, and for a nonlinear one it is accurate to second order — one order better than the EKF, and it captures the bias the EKF misses.

The classic place to see the difference is a polar-to-Cartesian measurement with a large bearing uncertainty — the true cloud bends into a “banana” that no single tangent can describe.

6When Gaussians aren't enough: the particle filter

Represent the whole distribution with samples — then it can be any shape at all.

EKF and UKF both still assume the answer is a single Gaussian bump. Some problems break that assumption outright. If a sensor measures , then and explain the data equally well and the posterior is genuinely bimodal — two peaks. No Gaussian can represent that. The particle filter throws away the Gaussian entirely and represents the distribution by a cloud of weighted samples (“particles”), which can take any shape.

The bootstrap particle filter

Carry particles with weights . Each step:

Predict: push every particle through the dynamics (with a random process-noise kick).
Update: reweight by the likelihood of the new measurement, , and normalize.
Resample: draw a fresh set of particles in proportion to the weights, so effort concentrates where the probability is — otherwise a few particles would hog all the weight and the rest would be dead wood.

As this converges to the exact Bayesian posterior, whatever its shape. The price is cost: you need many particles, especially in high dimensions.

7The family in one picture

Four filters, one recursion, each defined by the approximation it makes.

It is worth stepping back. Everything above is the same general Bayesian filter — predict with the dynamics, update with Bayes — and the four named filters differ only in how they keep that recursion tractable. That single fact is the most useful thing to carry away, because it tells you how to choose.

Kalman
linear dynamics and measurements, Gaussian noise. Exact, cheap, closed-form. Reach for it first and only leave it when forced.
EKF
mild nonlinearity, well-behaved near the estimate. Needs Jacobians. Decades of flight heritage; still the workhorse of navigation.
UKF
stronger nonlinearity, or when derivatives are awkward. No Jacobians, second-order accurate, same cost order as the EKF.
Particle
non-Gaussian or multimodal posteriors, severe nonlinearity. Handles anything, but costs the most and struggles in high dimensions.

83D in anger (A): radar target tracking

From range, azimuth and elevation to a clean 3D track.

Now the payoff. A radar at the origin sees a target through three nonlinear measurements — range , azimuth and elevation — each noisy. The state is 3D position and velocity, , propagated with a constant-velocity model. Because the measurement is nonlinear we use an EKF (or UKF); the angle innovations are wrapped to so a measurement at and a prediction at are treated as close.

The measurement and its Jacobian

Converting the raw straight to a Cartesian point gives a noisy scatter; the filter uses the dynamics to average those down and to estimate velocity. Here, with range noise and angle noise on a target passing near overhead, the raw points scatter by while the filtered track sits at and comes with a velocity estimate for free.

93D in anger (B): GNSS positioning

Where am I, and what time is it? Both at once, from satellite distances.

A GNSS receiver (GPS, Galileo, …) measures a pseudorange to each satellite it can see: the distance to the satellite, plus an unknown offset from the receiver's imperfect clock, plus noise, . The clock offset is shared by all satellites, so with enough of them the filter can solve for the receiver's 3D position and its clock error simultaneously — four unknowns, so four satellites minimum, more for accuracy. This is the “PNT” problem: positioning, navigation and timing from one set of measurements.

State and measurement

State : 3D position and velocity, clock bias and its drift (real receivers track both). The pseudorange to satellite and its gradient are An EKF with these line-of-sight rows fuses all satellites each step. With seven satellites and pseudorange noise the receiver is pinned to a few metres and its clock bias to a few metres (nanoseconds), tracked continuously as it moves and drifts.

103D in anger (C): data assimilation with the EnKF

How weather forecasts stay on track: thousands of states, one ensemble.

The last problem is the one that scales to millions of dimensions. When the state is a whole field — the atmosphere, the ocean, a cosmological density — you cannot store or invert a covariance matrix of that size. The Ensemble Kalman Filter represents the distribution by a modest ensemble of full model states (say 40–100 of them) and estimates the covariance from the scatter of the ensemble. The Kalman update is then applied using that sample covariance. This is the backbone of modern numerical weather prediction.

The ensemble Kalman update

With ensemble members , mean and anomalies , the sample forecast covariance is . The gain is the usual , and each member is updated with its own perturbed observation , , so the ensemble keeps a correct spread. A little “covariance inflation” stops the spread collapsing over time.

To show it in genuine 3D we use the Lorenz-63 system — the three coupled equations that gave us the word “butterfly effect.” It is chaotic: a free run from a slightly wrong start diverges completely within a few time units. We observe its three components noisily every so often and assimilate with 40 members.

11Caveats and limitations: tuning, consistency, divergence

A filter is only as good as the noise models you feed it.

Filters fail in characteristic ways, and all of them trace back to the two numbers and . Set the process noise too small and the filter believes its own model too much: it stops listening to data, its covariance shrinks to nothing, and when the truth does something unmodelled the estimate lags badly — worse, it is confident while being wrong. This is filter divergence, the classic failure. Set too large and the filter trusts every measurement, so the estimate just echoes the sensor noise.

How to tell if your filter is honest: consistency checks

A well-tuned filter's errors should match its claimed covariance. Two standard tests:

NEES (normalized estimation error squared), when you have ground truth: should average the state dimension and stay inside a band (this is panel (c) of the radar figure). NIS (normalized innovation squared), which needs no truth: should average the measurement dimension. If either runs consistently high, your filter is overconfident ( or too small); consistently low, it is underconfident. These are the diagnostics that turn filter tuning from guesswork into engineering.

Other ways filters fail

Wrong model: a constant-velocity filter cannot track a hard turn — add acceleration states or process noise. Linearization blow-up: an EKF near a singular geometry (a target straight overhead, where azimuth is undefined) can diverge; a UKF is more robust. Particle depletion: in high dimensions all but one particle get negligible weight — the filter collapses. Non-Gaussian noise: one outlier measurement can yank a Kalman filter hard, because least-squares has no defence against fat tails; robust gating or a heavier-tailed likelihood helps.

Conclusion — the main points, in plain English

If you remember five things from this note, make them these.
One loop
Every filter is predict (move forward, grow uncertainty) then update (fold in data, shrink uncertainty). Learn that loop and the rest is detail.
The gain
The Kalman gain is just a trust dial: measurement noise versus how unsure you already are. It blends prediction and measurement in exactly the right proportion.
Infer the unseen
Because the state's components become correlated, a filter estimates things it never measures — velocity from positions, a clock bias from distances.
Pick the simplest filter
Linear-Gaussian → Kalman. Mildly nonlinear → EKF. More so, or no derivatives → UKF. Multimodal or wild → particle. Fields too big to store → ensemble.
Be honest about uncertainty
A filter's covariance is a promise. Tune and , and check with NEES/NIS, so the promise is kept — an overconfident filter is dangerous precisely because it looks fine.

12Terminology

The words, in one place.
State
the quantity being estimated (position, velocity, clock bias, a whole field).
Process noise
how much the state can change unpredictably between steps; bigger = trust the model less.
Measurement noise
how noisy the sensor is; bigger = trust the data less.
Covariance
the filter's own estimate of how uncertain it is; a matrix of variances and correlations.
Innovation
measurement minus prediction, : the “surprise.” Its covariance is .
Kalman gain
how far to move the estimate toward the measurement; between “ignore it” and “believe it entirely.”
Jacobian
the matrix of partial derivatives used by the EKF to linearize a nonlinear model at the current estimate.
Sigma points
the few deterministic samples the UKF pushes through the nonlinear map instead of differentiating it.
Particles
weighted samples that represent an arbitrary (even multimodal) posterior in a particle filter.
Ensemble
a modest set of full model states whose scatter estimates the covariance in the EnKF.
NEES / NIS
consistency checks: is the filter's claimed uncertainty matched by its actual errors / innovations?
Divergence
when the estimate drifts from the truth while the filter stays (wrongly) confident — usually set too small.
Pseudorange
a GNSS distance measurement contaminated by the receiver's clock offset.
Data assimilation
filtering applied to a large physical field — weather, ocean, cosmology — usually with an ensemble.

Appendix A — the Kalman gain from first principles

Where actually comes from, worked in 1D.

The update is not a heuristic — it is the exact posterior of two Gaussians multiplied together. Take the 1D case. After predict we have a prior on the state, and a measurement model . Bayes says the posterior is proportional to prior likelihood:

The product of two Gaussians is Gaussian; collect the terms in . The posterior precision (inverse variance) is the sum of the two precisions, , and the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of the two centres, . A line of algebra turns these into the gain form:

So “blend by the gain” is “multiply the two Gaussians.” The multivariate result is the same calculation with matrices — and it is also the one step that minimises the posterior error variance, which is why the Kalman filter is the optimal linear estimator, Gaussian or not.

Appendix B — the matrix Kalman filter in code

The general recursion is nine lines. Here it is.

One predict–update step, any dimension

# predict
xh = F @ xh                  # move the mean forward with the dynamics
P  = F @ P @ F.T + Q         # grow the covariance by the process noise
# update
y  = z - H @ xh              # innovation: measurement minus prediction
S  = H @ P @ H.T + R         # innovation covariance
K  = P @ H.T @ inv(S)        # Kalman gain
xh = xh + K @ y              # correct the mean
P  = (I - K @ H) @ P         # shrink the covariance

For a nonlinear problem, swap the two lines that use F/H: use and for the mean, and the Jacobians everywhere a matrix is needed. That one change turns this Kalman filter into the EKF of §8 and §9.

Appendix C — the particle filter in code

Predict, weight, resample — the three lines that handle any distribution.

A bootstrap particle-filter step

# predict: push every particle through the dynamics (+ process noise)
X = f(X) + process_noise(size=X.shape)
# update: weight by the likelihood of the new measurement
w = likelihood(z, X)         # w_i  proportional to  p(z | x_i)
w /= w.sum()
# resample: draw N new particles in proportion to the weights
idx = systematic_resample(w)
X   = X[idx]

The resampling line is the heart of it: it draws new particles in proportion to their weights, so the cloud follows the probability. The effective sample size tells you how many particles are really doing work; when it drops too low you resample (or you are in trouble).

Appendix D — from Bayes to the recursion

Why “predict then update” is exactly Bayesian inference, done online.

The filtering density obeys an exact two-step recursion. The predict step is the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation — propagate the previous posterior through the dynamics:

The update step is Bayes' theorem — multiply by the likelihood of the new measurement and renormalize:

Everything in this note is a way of carrying these two integrals forward. If every density is Gaussian and every map linear, the integrals have a closed form and you get the Kalman filter exactly. Linearize the maps and you get the EKF; approximate the Gaussian integral with sigma points and you get the UKF; approximate the densities with samples and you get the particle filter; approximate them with an ensemble and you get the EnKF. Four filters, one equation — which is the whole point of this note.
